title: Accounting for Bonus Issue and Right Issue
outcomes: Explain a bonus issue as capitalisation of profits and compute bonus entitlements.
Apply section 63 — permitted sources, conditions and restrictions — and journalise bonus issues, including making partly paid shares fully paid.
Explain the effects of a bonus issue on capital, reserves and per-share figures.
Explain a rights issue under section 62(1)(a), its exceptions and the right of renunciation.
Compute book value, theoretical ex-right price and value of a right, and journalise a rights issue.
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of a rights issue.

meta.exam_tip: Bonus questions usually say "minimum reduction in free reserves" — use CRR and (cash-realised) securities premium first. Rights questions test the ex-right price and value of right.

concepts.title: Bonus issue — capitalisation of profits
body: A bonus issue gives existing shareholders additional fully paid shares at no cost, in proportion to their present holding (e.g., 2 bonus shares for every 3 held: a holder of 6,000 gets 4,000 and ends with 10,000).

No new money is raised. Reserves that could have been paid out as dividend are converted into paid-up capital — hence "capitalisation of profits". The number of shares rises, but net worth is unchanged and each holder's percentage stays the same.

If the bonus would take paid-up capital beyond authorised capital, the company first increases its authorised capital by resolution in general meeting. A return of allotment with a copy of the resolution is filed with the Registrar.
concepts.analogy: Cutting a pizza into more slices: you have more pieces, but not more pizza.
concepts.work: For listed clients a CA checks the bonus ratio, the record date and the sources used, and recomputes EPS for all periods presented, since a bonus changes share count retrospectively.

concepts.title: Sources for bonus — section 63(1) and Table F
body: Fully paid bonus shares may be issued out of free reserves, the securities premium balance, or the capital redemption reserve. Reserves created by revaluation of assets can never be capitalised.

Free reserves (s. 2(43)) are reserves available for dividend as per the latest audited balance sheet; unrealised or notional gains, revaluation, and fair-value changes recognised in equity are excluded.

Securities premium and CRR may be used only for issuing unissued shares as fully paid bonus shares — not for paying up unpaid amounts on existing partly paid shares. Free reserves can be used for both (Table F, para 39).
SEBI requires a listed company to use only securities premium realised in cash; an unlisted company may use premium arising from non-cash issues too.
concepts.analogy: Three wallets may pay for bonus shares (free reserves, securities premium, CRR); the "revaluation" wallet holds only paper gains, so it is locked.
concepts.work: A typical audit check: did the company use revaluation reserve or non-cash premium (if listed) for a bonus? Either is a violation that must be reported.

concepts.title: Conditions for a bonus issue — section 63(2) and (3)
body: A company may capitalise profits or reserves for bonus only if: (a) its articles authorise it; (b) it is authorised in general meeting on the board's recommendation; (c) there is no default in paying interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities; (d) it has not defaulted on statutory dues of employees such as PF, gratuity and bonus; (e) partly paid shares outstanding on the allotment date are made fully paid; (f) it meets any other prescribed conditions.
Bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend (s. 63(3)). Once the board has announced a bonus recommendation, it cannot be withdrawn.
concepts.analogy: A bonus is like a family celebration — you must first clear the dues you owe to lenders and to the staff before you can hand out gifts.
concepts.work: Before certifying a bonus, the company secretary and auditors check default status on deposits, debt securities and PF/gratuity — a single default blocks the issue.

concepts.title: Journal entries and effects of a bonus issue
body: Fully paid bonus: (1) Capital Redemption Reserve / Securities Premium / General Reserve / Profit and Loss A/c Dr, To Bonus to Shareholders A/c; (2) Bonus to Shareholders A/c Dr, To Share Capital A/c.

Making partly paid shares fully paid (free reserves only): (1) General Reserve / Profit and Loss Dr, To Bonus to Shareholders; (2) Share Final Call Dr, To Share Capital; (3) Bonus to Shareholders Dr, To Share Final Call.
"Minimum reduction in free reserves" means use CRR and (eligible) securities premium first, then free reserves.

Effects: share capital up, accumulated reserves down by the same amount; net worth unchanged; EPS and other per-share values fall; market price adjusts downward; the market usually treats a bonus as a favourable sign.
concepts.analogy: Moving money from your savings jar to a locked jar labelled "capital" — your total money is the same, only the label changes.
concepts.work: After a bonus, analysts restate per-share data (EPS, dividend per share) so trends remain comparable — a routine task in equity research.

concepts.title: Rights issue — section 62(1)(a) and its exceptions
body: When a company (public or private) wants to increase subscribed capital by issuing further shares, it must first offer them to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holding, so their control and governance rights are not diluted.

Letter of offer: states the number of shares and a period of not less than 15 days and not more than 30 days, after which the offer is deemed declined. Unless the articles provide otherwise, the shareholder may renounce the shares in favour of any other person. After the period (or on an earlier refusal), the board may dispose of the shares in a manner not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company.

Exceptions (further shares need not be offered to existing holders): with a special resolution, to employees under an ESOP scheme; with a special resolution, to any persons for cash or other consideration at a price fixed by a registered valuer's report; on exercise of a conversion option attached to debentures or loans, if the terms were approved by special resolution before the issue (s. 62(3)); and where the Government directs conversion of its loans or debentures into shares in public interest (s. 62(4)).
concepts.analogy: Like a housing society offering a new parking slot first to existing residents in proportion to their flats before advertising it outside.
concepts.work: Company law advisers draft the letter of offer, track the 15–30 day window, and record renunciations — errors here can make the allotment invalid.

concepts.title: Pricing a rights issue — book value, cum-right, ex-right and value of right
body: Book value per share = net worth ÷ number of shares. Net worth (s. 2(57)) is paid-up capital plus reserves from profits and securities premium, less accumulated losses and unwritten-off deferred or miscellaneous expenditure; revaluation reserves, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation reserves are excluded. Market value can differ from book value.
Cum-right price: market price before the rights issue. Rights are usually offered below market price to attract response and reward existing holders.
Theoretical ex-right price (TERP) = (cum-right price × existing shares + issue price × rights shares) ÷ (existing shares + rights shares).

Value of right per existing share = cum-right price − TERP. Value of right per rights share = TERP − issue price. A holder who renounces sells this value; one who subscribes keeps it in the shares; one who ignores the offer loses it.
concepts.analogy: If a fruit seller mixes 4 mangoes worth ₹60 each with 1 mango bought at ₹45, the "average" mango is worth ₹57 — that is the ex-right price.
concepts.work: Investment bankers and research analysts compute TERP to advise clients whether to subscribe, renounce or sell entitlements in the market.

concepts.title: Accounting for rights issue; advantages and disadvantages
body: Entry: debit Bank A/c; credit Equity Share Capital A/c with face value and Securities Premium A/c with any premium. If money is collected in instalments, application/allotment accounts are used exactly as for any share issue.
A rights issue raises net worth and cash by (rights shares × issue price). Shares cannot be issued at a discount except as the law permits.

Advantages: existing holders keep their proportion and control; it deters management from issuing shares to friendly parties; holders are compensated for dilution by the lower price (or by selling the right); it saves the heavy expenses of a public issue; it is viewed positively; it has a better chance of success and is easier to handle.
Disadvantages: it dilutes the market value per share; the attractive price must be judged against the share's true worth.
concepts.analogy: A rights issue is a "members first" sale: discounted for those already in, with the option to hand your coupon to someone else.
concepts.work: In due-diligence, the CA confirms that rights shares were allotted in the offer ratio and that renunciations were recorded correctly in the register of members.

solution.text: Bonus shares = 60,000 ÷ 3 = 20,000 = ₹2,00,000. Use CRR ₹40,000 and cash-realised premium ₹30,000 first (not free reserves). Balance ₹1,30,000 from general reserve. Non-cash premium cannot be used by a listed company (SEBI) and revaluation reserve cannot be used by any company.

illustrations.q: Kanak Ltd has 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 paid up. Securities premium ₹60,000; general reserve ₹1,50,000. The company decides (i) to make the shares fully paid by a final call of ₹2 met out of general reserve, and (ii) then to issue fully paid bonus shares of one for every four held, using securities premium first. Journalise.

solution.title: Why general reserve for step (i)?
solution.text: Securities premium and CRR can be applied only to issue new fully paid bonus shares, not to pay unpaid amounts on existing shares. Free reserves such as general reserve can do both.

solution.text: One for four on 40,000 = 10,000 shares = ₹1,00,000: securities premium ₹60,000 + general reserve ₹40,000. General reserve left = 1,50,000 − 80,000 − 40,000 = ₹30,000.

jobs.title: Board note on a proposed bonus issue
jobs.role: Finance manager of a listed mid-cap company
jobs.situation: The board wants a 1:1 bonus. Equity capital is ₹20 crore; CRR ₹2 crore; securities premium ₹12 crore (of which ₹3 crore arose on a share-swap acquisition); general reserve ₹15 crore; revaluation reserve ₹8 crore. Authorised capital is ₹30 crore.
steps: Eligible sources for a listed company: CRR ₹2 crore + cash-realised premium ₹9 crore + general reserve ₹9 crore.
Exclude revaluation reserve and the ₹3 crore non-cash premium.
Authorised capital must rise to at least ₹40 crore before allotment — propose the resolution.
Confirm no default on deposits, debt securities or employee statutory dues, and that there are no partly paid shares.
jobs.takeaway: A bonus note must show both the arithmetic of sources and the legal checklist of s. 63.

checks.label: Minimum authorised capital after bonus (₹ crore)

jobs.title: Advising a client on a rights entitlement
jobs.role: Practising CA advising an individual investor
jobs.situation: A client holds 2,000 shares of a company announcing a 1:5 rights issue at ₹180 when the share trades at ₹240. She has no spare cash and asks what to do.
steps: Value per rights share = 230 − 180 = ₹50; she is entitled to 400 rights.
If she ignores the offer, her shares lose ₹10 each (₹20,000 in all).
Advise her to renounce (sell) the entitlement for about ₹20,000, which offsets the fall.
Mention tax treatment of sale of rights entitlement as a separate point to check.
jobs.takeaway: Doing nothing in a rights issue is the only option that loses money.

options: Default in payment of PF contribution to employees
mcqs.explain: Default on statutory dues of employees (PF, gratuity, bonus) is a bar under s. 63(2)(d).

options: Cannot be issued in lieu of dividend
mcqs.explain: They cannot replace dividend and, once announced, cannot be withdrawn; they are always fully paid.

mcqs.explain: The notice fixes a period of 15 to 30 days from the date of offer.

model.title: Working
model.text: Bonus shares = 80,000 × 2/5 = 32,000 = ₹3,20,000. Sources in order: CRR ₹90,000; securities premium realised in cash ₹50,000 (the ₹25,000 non-cash premium cannot be used by a listed company); general reserve ₹1,80,000. remarks: Most candidates used the full ₹75,000 premium — the SEBI cash-realisation condition was overlooked.

questions.q: State the sources out of which bonus shares can be issued and the conditions a company must satisfy under section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013.

model.text: Sources (s. 63(1)): free reserves; securities premium account; capital redemption reserve account. Reserves created by revaluation of assets cannot be capitalised.

items: Authorised in general meeting on the recommendation of the board.
No default in payment of interest or principal on fixed deposits or debt securities.
No default in statutory dues of employees such as PF, gratuity and bonus.
Partly paid shares outstanding on the date of allotment made fully paid.
Bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of dividend; a bonus announced by the board cannot be withdrawn.

viva.q: What is a bonus issue, and why is it called capitalisation of profits?
viva.model: A bonus issue is an issue of fully paid shares to existing shareholders free of cost, in proportion to the shares they already hold. No new money comes into the company. It is called capitalisation of profits because accumulated profits or reserves, which could otherwise be paid as dividend, are converted into paid-up share capital. Net worth does not change, and each shareholder's percentage holding stays the same.

viva.q: What is a rights issue, and what does section 62(1)(a) require in the letter of offer?
viva.model: A rights issue is an offer of new shares to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their present holding, so that they can keep their percentage in the company. Under section 62(1)(a) the offer is made by a notice stating the number of shares offered and a time limit of not less than fifteen days and not more than thirty days, after which it is treated as declined. Unless the articles say otherwise, the shareholder can renounce the shares in favour of anyone else. After the period, the board may dispose of unaccepted shares in a way not disadvantageous to the shareholders and the company.

viva.q: How do you calculate the theoretical ex-right price and the value of a right?
viva.model: The theoretical ex-right price equals the cum-right market value of the existing shares plus the amount paid for the rights shares, divided by the total number of shares after the issue, that is existing plus rights shares. The value of a right per existing share is the cum-right price minus the ex-right price. Per rights share, it is the ex-right price minus the issue price.

viva.q: What are the effects of a bonus issue on the company's accounts and on per-share figures?
viva.model: Share capital increases and reserves decrease by the same amount, so net worth and total assets do not change. The number of shares goes up, so earnings per share, book value per share and the market price per share fall, though each shareholder's total holding value is broadly the same. The market generally sees a bonus issue as a favourable signal.

cases.title: Arohi Electronics — bonus followed by rights
cases.case: Arohi Electronics Ltd (listed) has 3,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully paid. Reserves: general reserve ₹9,00,000, securities premium (all realised in cash) ₹4,00,000, revaluation reserve ₹5,00,000. It first issues bonus shares of 1 for 5, using securities premium first. After the bonus, it offers rights shares of 1 for 4 at ₹40 each. The market price just before the rights issue (cum-right) is ₹65. Kabir holds 1,500 shares before the bonus.

mcqs.q: How many bonus shares does Kabir receive and how many does he hold after the bonus?
How much general reserve is used for the bonus?
mcqs.explain: Bonus = 60,000 shares × ₹10 = ₹6,00,000. Securities premium ₹4,00,000 is used first; general reserve ₹2,00,000. Revaluation reserve cannot be used.

mcqs.q: What is the theoretical ex-right price?
What can Kabir obtain by renouncing all his rights?
mcqs.explain: Kabir gets 1,800 ÷ 4 = 450 rights. Value per right share = 60 − 40 = ₹20; 450 × 20 = ₹9,000 (equal to 1,800 × ₹5 lost per existing share).

mcqs.q: The rights issue entry for the whole company credits Securities Premium with:

summary: Bonus = free fully paid shares to existing holders pro rata; capitalisation of profits; net worth unchanged.
Sources (s. 63(1)): free reserves, securities premium, CRR — never revaluation reserve. Listed companies: only cash-realised premium (SEBI).
Partly paid shares can be made fully paid only from free reserves.

Conditions (s. 63(2)): articles, GM approval on board recommendation, no default on deposits/debt securities or employee dues, partly paid shares made fully paid; not in lieu of dividend; no withdrawal once announced.
Rights (s. 62(1)(a)): offer to existing holders pro rata, 15–30 days, renounceable unless articles prohibit.
TERP = (cum-right price × existing + issue price × rights) ÷ total shares; value of right = cum-right − TERP (per existing share).
remember: Bonus entry passes through Bonus to Shareholders A/c.
"Minimum reduction in free reserves" → CRR and eligible premium first.
A rights issue increases net worth; a bonus issue does not.
traps: Using revaluation reserve or non-cash premium (listed) for bonus.
Using securities premium to pay up partly paid shares.
